sections.md: # Welcome to Tangible!

When founding Tangible, careful thought was given to “what would set this practice apart?”. Ultimately the idea was to create a practice that moves away from theoretical and instead connects clients with their emotions in practical ways. At Tangible our Mantra is *Helping people* ***feel*** *better.* We place an emphasis on creating healing that our clients can feel by connecting them with their emotions through tangible skills.

Good therapy starts with good therapists. We believe in our team and are selective only to bring in therapists which we believe can be great. Our approach to creating good therapy is to emphasize training and development with all of our therapists. We don’t want perfect therapists, we want therapists who strive to improve for the sake of themselves and their clients. We hope that your experience here will be one of pride, growth, and satisfaction in your work.
**IN THIS LESSON**
## How to maintain client confidentiality and trust.

Confidentiality is one of the guiding values of our profession, we want to ensure that private information about clients, employees, partners and our company is well-protected. Examples of confidential information are:

● Employee records

● Unpublished financial information

● All client information

● Unpublished company goals, forecasts, and initiatives marked as confidential

We expect you to act responsibly when handling confidential information.

You must:

● Lock or secure confidential information at all times.

● Shred confidential documents when they’re no longer needed.

● Make sure you view confidential information on secure, password-protected devices only.

● Only disclose information to other employees when it’s necessary and authorized.

● Keep confidential documents inside our company’s premises unless it’s absolutely necessary to move them.

You must not:

● Use confidential information for your personal benefit or profit.

● Disclose confidential information to anyone outside of our company.

● Replicate confidential documents and files and store them on insecure devices.

**IN THIS LESSON**

## How to navigate hours, time off, and getting sick.
# Attendance

Tangible expects you to be present during your scheduled working hours. If you face an emergency that prevents you from coming to work, you are responsible for ensuring any impacted parties (including clients) are notified. All absences should be reported to your direct supervisor via text or email. It is important that we create a calm, consistent environment for our clients and employees. Repeated absenteeism impacts this environment, and may be cause for termination.

Due to the nature of our work, employee work schedules are highly individualized and should be coordinated with your direct supervisor. Any changes to your regular work hours should be approved by your direct supervisor.
# Time Off

Paid-time off (PTO) is offered to all full-time employees. PTO is accrued at a rate of 80 hours per year averaged over a 27 hr work week. Meaning additional hours worked above that accrue PTO at a quicker rate. PTO does not reset and will roll-over into the new year. PTO is capped at 80 hours and accrual will stop if you reach that cap. PTO must be used to be paid out, PTO is not paid out upon termination. If you are taking PTO then it should be submitted on your time card. Time off not submitted will be assumed as VTO.

Unpaid time off or voluntary time off (VTO)is available at all times to employees. Employees may take VTO when PTO is not available or may choose to take VTO in place of PTO.

Work-life balance is important and employees are encouraged to take time for themselves throughout the year. All scheduled time off should be approved by your direct supervisor with at least two weeks’ notice to ensure clients are being appropriately managed. There are no limits on time off however time off that is excessive may impact clients negatively. Excessive time off could include time off that exceeds two consecutive weeks or that is too frequent. Plan time off in a way that makes sense for both you and your clients. Time off that impacts the quality of care may result in disciplinary action.
# Holidays

Employees are welcome to arrange their schedule to take unpaid time off on all federal holidays, or to use PTO for the day if they have it. If an employee does choose to work on a holiday, compensation remains the same as a regular work day.
# Sickness, Bereavement, & Parental Leave

Employees do not receive paid sick or bereavement leave (full-time employees may use their PTO), however, we hope to support you in taking needed time off when you are unwell or grieving. You can take sick leave to recover from short-term illness, injuries, mental issues, and other indisposition. If you have the flu or other contagious disease, please avoid coming into the office by taking time off or seeing your clients by telehealth. Telehealth is an option, not a requirement.

Our company offers three months of unpaid parental leave. If you are about to be a new parent (either through childbirth or adoption), talk to your direct supervisor to arrange your leave. Please give us at least three months' notice before your leave begins.

**IN THIS LESSON**

## You’ve put in the hours, now it’s time to get paid.
# Pay Periods

Payroll is processed bi-weekly, meaning you get paid every two weeks. Pay periods close one week before payroll is processed on Friday. Hours should be submitted into the payroll form at the end of every pay period. Payments are sent out via direct deposit to your bank account.

Our calendar is your time card. Ensure that your calendar is an accurate reflection of your hours at the end of the day so you can count your hours correctly each pay period. Cancellations, reschedules and any other adjustments to a calendar should be changed within the same day that the request is made in order to ensure accuracy.
# Counting Your Hours

Pay is calculated based on billable hours (sessions) and required meetings, including supervision if supervised in-house. Outside supervision costs will be covered, but do not count towards billable hours. Billable hours include all sessions completed with a client, no-shows, and late-cancellations. Notes, CEUs, and other outside-of-session learning does not count towards your hours.

If you have a concern or question about payroll, please direct those questions to your supervisor.
# No Show Policy

We have a 24-hour cancellation policy that is communicated thoroughly with our clients. You as the therapist decide whether a client is charged for a no-show or a late cancellation, and billing charges exactly what you set in Simple Practice. To charge, set the status to No show or Late canceled and change the Appointment Fee to $75. If you're not charging (for example, the client cancelled because they're sick), set the status to Canceled instead. You will only be paid for sessions for which the fee is charged. Sessions canceled in advance or sessions that are rescheduled do not count as billable hours.

To count a no-show, you must wait for the client for at least 15 minutes and reach out to the client to confirm they are not coming for their appointment. You can reach out to them directly or ask the reception team to do so.
# How to Submit Hours

At the end of each pay period, you are responsible for submitting your hours. If hours are not submitted before payroll is processed, then those hours will need to be paid out at the following pay period. We want you to get paid so please submit those hours on time!

To submit your hours, you can do so through the employee portal under the submit hours link or via the Slack reminder.

**IN THIS LESSON**

## The perks of working at Tangible.
# Employment Status

Employment status is determined by the amount of billable hours worked in a given pay period. Employees are considered full-time when they are at or above 50 billable hours across a pay period. Due to cancellations, this will often mean averaging 27-28 scheduled clients per week. Employees who are below this limit are considered part-time employees.

Our benefits below are labeled as to whether benefits apply to all employees or just full-time employees.
#### All Employees
# Workers Compensation

We strive to keep our workplace safe, but accidents may happen occasionally. Employees who are injured at work (by accident or disease) can receive wage replacement, medical care and rehabilitation benefits according to workers’ compensation laws, when appropriate.

Please inform us of your injury as soon as possible. Ask your supervisor for forms that you need to file a claim or contact your state agency for workers’ compensation. Our company has a workers’ compensation policy according to the guidelines of the state of Utah.
#### All Employees
# Malpractice Insurance

At Tangible Therapy, we believe that when therapists feel secure, they can do their best work. That’s why we provide malpractice insurance as a core benefit, at no extra cost. This ensures our clinicians are protected legally and professionally, freeing them to focus fully on what matters most: supporting their clients. With liability coverage built in, our team can work with confidence, knowing we have their backs.
#### Full-Time Employees
# Health Insurance

Your health is essential, not just to the work you do but to your life. That’s why we provide a flexible option to ensure you can get coverage that makes sense for you. Our health insurance benefit offers up to $500 a month of reimbursement towards a health insurance premium. This allows you to go to the marketplace and find a plan that best fits your needs.

If you receive health insurance through a parent or spouse, you may also get reimbursed for that premium. Once you’ve reached full time hours, submit a picture of a health insurance premium receipt to your supervisor and we will add it to your paychecks.
#### Full-Time Employees
# Paid Time Off

We know that great therapy starts with well-rested, balanced clinicians. That’s why Tangible Therapy offers Paid Time Off (PTO) to all our therapists. Whether it's for rest, travel, family time, or simply recharging, we encourage time away from work as a vital part of sustaining meaningful clinical care. You can learn more about using your PTO benefits in the attendance section.
#### All Employees
# 401k Plan

We’re not just thinking about today, we’re helping you plan for tomorrow. Our 401(k) retirement plans empower you to build long-term financial security with ease. With **employer contributions**  and flexible investment options, it’s our way of supporting your future goals while you support others in the present.

Our 401k plan includes a 100% match for the first 3% of contributions and 50% of the next 2%. Meaning if you would like to receive the full company match, you contribute 5% of your paycheck and we will match you 4%.

All employees, full-time and part-time, may start contributing to the 401k after working at Tangible for 3 months.
**IN THIS LESSON**
# We work here, let’s make this a place we all want to work.

### Equal opportunity employment

Tangible Mental Health is an equal-opportunity employer. We don’t tolerate discrimination against protected characteristics (gender, age, sexual orientation, race, nationality, ethnicity, religion, disability, veteran status.) We expect all employees to treat others with respect and professionalism. We commit to penalizing discriminatory, offensive, or inappropriate behavior. To do this properly, we ask you to report any discriminatory action against yourself or your colleagues to your direct supervisor. Our company will not retaliate against you if you file a complaint. Any employee who retaliates or discriminates will face disciplinary action

### Harassment and Violence

Tangible believes in creating a safe work environment for its employees. Employees should be mindful of jokes, comments and actions and how they may impact or be perceived by those around them. Behaviors that create an unsafe work environment for others (clients or coworkers) will not be tolerated. Sexual harassment of any sort is strictly prohibited. If you’re being harassed, whether by a colleague, customer or vendor, please talk to your supervisor.

### Dress Code

What we wear is often a client's first indication of our professional standard. Tangible asks that all employees show up in professional, business casual attire. Your supervisor may provide you with further guidance on workplace dress at their discretion to ensure our environment remains professional and client-centered.

### Cyber security and digital devices

This section deals with all things digital at work. We want to set some guidelines for using computers, phones, our internet connection and social media to ensure security and protect our assets.

#### Internet usage

Our corporate internet connection is primarily for business. But, you can occasionally use our connection for personal purposes as long as they don’t interfere with your job responsibilities. Also, we expect you to temporarily halt personal activities that slow down our internet connection (e.g. uploading photos) if you’re asked to. For security purposes, please do not share our wifi password with clients.

You must not use our internet connection to:

- Download or upload obscene, offensive or illegal material.
- Send confidential information to unauthorized recipients.
- Invade another person’s privacy and gain access to sensitive information.
- Download or upload pirated movies, music, material or software.
- Visit potentially dangerous websites that can compromise our network and computers’ safety.
- Perform unauthorized or illegal actions, like hacking, fraud or buying/selling illegal goods.

#### Corporate email

Email is essential to our work. You should use your company email primarily for work, but we allow some uses of your company email for personal reasons.

- **Work-related use.** You can use your corporate email for work-related purposes without limitations. For example, you can sign up for newsletters and online services that will help you in your job or professional growth.
- **Personal use.** You can use your email for personal reasons as long as you keep it safe, and avoid spamming and disclosing confidential information. For example, you can send emails to friends and family and download ebooks, guides and other safe content for your personal use.

Our general expectations

No matter how you use your corporate email, we expect you to avoid:

- Signing up for illegal, unreliable, disreputable or suspect websites and services.
- Sending unauthorized marketing content or emails.
- Sending insulting or discriminatory messages and content.
- Intentionally spamming other people’s emails, including your coworkers.

In general, use strong passwords and be vigilant in catching emails that carry malware or phishing attempts.

#### Social Media

Remember that you are a professional and your online presence should be reflective of that. Clients will look up your personal accounts via Google. Be mindful of what is publicly shared through your accounts and how it reflects on you.

Employees are permitted to access personal accounts at work. But, we expect you to act responsibly, according to our policies, and ensure that you stay productive. Specifically, we ask you to:

- Ensure others know that your personal account or statements don’t represent our company.
- Avoid sharing intellectual property (e.g trademarks) or confidential information. Ask your manager first before you share company news that’s not officially announced.
- Avoid any defamatory, offensive or derogatory content. You may violate our company’s anti-harassment policy if you direct such content towards colleagues, clients or partners.

### Company-issued equipment

Unless otherwise mentioned in your contract, any equipment we offer belongs to our company and you may not sell it or give it away. You are also responsible for keeping our equipment safe and in good working condition. If your equipment breaks or malfunctions, let us know so we can arrange to get it repaired.

#### Theft and damage

Our equipment is insured for theft and damage. Please let us know within 24 hours if your equipment is stolen or damaged. We might be able to trace stolen laptops and cell phones. Please also file a theft statement (affidavit) with the police and give us a copy.

#### Keeping devices secure

Keep your company-issued computer, tablet and cell phone secure:

- Keep all devices password-protected.
- Don’t leave your devices unattended.
- Install security updates for browsers and other systems as soon as updates are available.
- Log into company accounts and systems through secure and private networks only.

### Employee relationships

#### Fraternization

Fraternization refers to dating or being friends with your colleagues. In this policy, “dating” equals consensual romantic relationships and sexual relations. Non-consensual relationships constitute sexual violence and we prohibit them explicitly. If you start dating a colleague, we expect you to maintain professionalism and keep personal discussions outside of our workplace. You are also obliged to respect your colleagues who date each other. We won’t tolerate sexual jokes, malicious gossip, and improper comments. If you witness this kind of behavior, please report it to your supervisor.

#### Dating managers

To avoid accusations of favoritism, abuse of authority and sexual harassment, supervisors must not date their direct reports. This restriction extends to every manager above an employee.

### Conflict of Interest

Conflicts of interest occur when your interests are placed at odds with the clients or the company’s. Conflicts of interest can have serious consequences or interfere with the care of our clients. We expect you to be vigilant to spot circumstances that create conflicts of interest, either to yourself or for your direct reports. If you are experiencing an ethical dilemma, talk to your direct supervisor and we will try to help you resolve it.
**IN THIS LESSON**
# Scheduling new clients and navigating cancellations.
# Scheduling

When your calendar is structured, your mind can be more present, your energy better paced, and your sessions more grounded. Good scheduling isn't just about logistics—it's about protecting your capacity and showing up with consistency and care.

Clear, predictable scheduling helps clients feel secure and respected. It minimizes confusion, reduces no-shows, and reinforces the professional boundaries that support therapeutic safety. Behind the scenes, strong organizational systems, like digital calendars, reminders, and checklists, help you manage your caseload, documentation, billing, and personal time without constant overwhelm..
# New Clients

Reception handles all incoming appointment calls. There will be times that a client requests a 15-minute consultation call to determine if a therapist is the right fit. If this happens, reception will schedule an appointment with the client's contact info and set a time for that call. We will address how to do these calls later in this training.
# Client Portal

Clients are sent a link via email when they schedule their first appointment. the link is for their client portal where clients can access onboarding docs, practice policies, billing docs and pay invoices. Clients can access their client portal at any time at tangiblementalhealth.com.

Clients must have **ALL** of their documents filled out before the first session. Our reception team will remind them and check on this but you are responsible for checking that docs are filled out before your first session. This can be seen under the clients tab in Simple Practice, under the section labeled files. If clients don’t have their files filled out please inform to do so before you meet with them, even if they are already at the practice.

*The most common thing clients forget to fill out are insurance info and credit card info, this is why we ask them to fill it out before the first session.
# Cancellation Policy

In the client intake docs, our clients agree to our cancellation policy. This policy requires clients to give 24 hours' notice of cancellation or they will be charged a $75 cancellation fee. Insurance will not cover this bill. The only exception is illness: we don't charge clients who cancel because they're sick, because we don't want them coming in sick. Clients that fail to show up for their appointment aka. No shows also fall under this category as we have not received adequate notice of their absence. The client is reminded of this policy each week in their reminder text/email that reminds them of their appointment.

In order to count a no show, you must wait for the client to show for at least 15-minutes in the office or in the virtual office. You must also reach out to the client to confirm that the client will not be attending during those 15 minutes. You can reach out directly or you can have the reception team reach out.

You ultimately get to decide if you charge your clients for No Show/Late Cancellation, but you will not be paid for sessions that you do not charge for. Our billing department charges exactly what you set in Simple Practice:

- **To charge the fee:** set the status to **No show** or **Late canceled**, then change the **Appointment Fee** to **$75**. The fee does not change on its own when you change the status.
- **To not charge** (including when a client cancels because they're sick): set the status to **Canceled** (client cancelled), not Late canceled.

If you charge a no show or late cancel fee, please communicate that with the client.

Billing/payroll is determined by the clients' attendance status on your Simple Practice calendar. You can adjust the clients' attendance status with the green drop-down menu that appears just below their name when their appointment is selected. Please ensure all attendance changes are noted on simple practice ***the day of the session***  so that billing can be made accurately.

Note: Billing insurance for sessions where the client is not present is considered insurance fraud, please ensure your attendance status is kept accurate.
# Scheduling Future Sessions

After the first session, you are responsible for the ongoing maintenance of your schedule with clients. You are welcome to reach out to the reception team if you need help canceling appointments or reaching a client but your schedule is yours to own.

When scheduling a client, we should have a slot mindset rather than a week-to-week mindset, meaning we try to see the same client at the same time each week. “Debbie on Mondays at 4pm”

Scheduling week to week will happen at times due to unforeseen circumstances but it’s best to be avoided when possible. The best practice is to schedule out 8-10 sessions using the repeat feature. This makes it easy for the reception team to see future openings.
**IN THIS LESSON**
# How we handle charging our clients.

### Informing our clients

Our billing department is responsible for all billing-related concerns but therapists play an important role in informing our clients about our billing policies. Below is how billing works, so you can explain it in general terms. In the first session, check whether the client knows what their sessions will cost; questions about a client’s costs or payments go to the billing department.

- All cash-pay clients will be placed on autopay and charged within 24 hours of sessions
- All insurance paid claims will be sent to the client's insurance, we will then charge them when the insurance returns the claim. (Usually 2-4 weeks) If they have a copay it will be established at that time and be charged in tandem via autopay with sessions going forward.
- Invoices the client receives will be via the email they used to create their account and payments can be made through their client portal at Tangiblementalhealth.com
- Some clients (rare exceptions) may ask to be informed before being charged. Usually, this will happen during the first session or two and then they know what to expect. If so, please inform our billing manager.
- If a client has any billing concerns please direct them to our billing department which they can call through our main number.

### Submitting Insurance Claims

Our billing manager will be responsible for submitting all insurance claims. In order to submit claims, the client will need a diagnosis. If you feel uncertain about giving one to the client, utilize an unspecified modifier with the diagnosis that is the closest fit. Once you feel more certain then feel free to change the diagnosis. The unfortunate truth is that most insurances will not pay for an adjustment disorder diagnosis. Every client's diagnosis must be entered in Simple Practice **the same day** you see them for their first session. Our billing manager may reach out to you if a client is missing a diagnosis.

### CPT Codes (Appointment Codes)

CPT codes are how the insurance company knows what type of service we are billing for. We need to verify the accuracy of our CPT codes whenever we are inputting a new session onto the calendar.

- 90791 Psychiatric Diagnostic Evaluation — Used for the first session we meet with a client
- 90837 Psychotherapy, 60 min — Used for all regular sessions.
- 90853 Group Therapy — Used for group therapy sessions
- 90785 Psytx Complex Interactive — Used as an additional code when billing 90837 already. Should be used in instances where additional work is being done to coordinate care for the client outside of the session or with a third party such as talking with parents, filling out documentation, speaking with other providers.

### Cash Pay Scale

If a client is not using insurance and asks if there is a discount for cash pay, generally the answer is “no”. If you are aware of extreme circumstances for the client or if this is a client whose insurance has changed and they would like to keep meeting with you, you can slide down to as low as $115 per session.

### Our Rates

$175 per session (Insurance rates are determined by the insurance company and are typically closer to $110)

$30 per group therapy session

$25 per page documentation fee — If ever you complete documentation for a client such as accommodation forms, professional letters, ESA letters, please reach out to the billing department and let them know to charge this fee.
**IN THIS LESSON**
## Protecting ourselves and ensuring insurance coverage
# Why do we document?

Keeping thorough, accurate documentation isn’t just a legal or ethical requirement, it’s a vital part of responsible, effective clinical care. Well-written notes help track a client’s progress, clarify treatment goals, and guide your clinical decisions over time. They provide continuity in care, especially when revisiting past themes or adjusting your approach.

Good documentation also protects you and your clients. In the event of an audit, insurance request, or legal issue, clear records demonstrate professionalism, accountability, and adherence to best practices. Beyond that, notes can support self-reflection and improve the quality of your work by making patterns and insights more visible over time. Ultimately, documentation is an extension of the care you offer in session.
# Notes

There are two types of notes in simple practice, the progress note and the psychotherapy note. The progress note is important for ensuring proper procedure was followed and to provide justification of care to insurance when requested. The psychotherapy note is a separate note that allows you to note important things to yourself before the next session. This is not included in requests by insurance companies or legal teams.

The progress note should be kept as accurate as possible. All notes should be completed within 72 hours of meeting with the client. If safety concerns arise in session such as suicidal or homicidal ideation, self-harm, abuse, neglect, etc., the note must be completed within **24 hours**, and it should document the concern as well as any steps you took to address that issue. In the case of mandatory reporting, return to the note after making your report to document who you spoke with and the case number if applicable.

When filling out notes select the Tangible Progress Note in the drop-down menu. Fill in the prompts on the page. The first note will take the longest. Going forward you can reload the previous note and change the information as needed.
# Treatment Plans

A treatment plan is more than paperwork, it’s the roadmap that guides the therapeutic journey. It brings structure, clarity, and direction to the work, helping both the therapist and the client stay focused and aligned. With a strong treatment plan, goals become visible, interventions become intentional, and progress becomes measurable.

Each client is required to have a treatment plan within a week of their second session. Use the **Basic** treatment plan template in Simple Practice (under Simple Practice templates) for every client. Each plan should include clear goals as to what the client should get out of their time at Tangible. The goals should be measurable. The plan should also clearly outline the interventions you plan to use to get the client to that goal.
**IN THIS LESSON**
# How to respond effectively in a crisis situation.

## Risk of Harm

Our ethical responsibility to clients is to maintain confidentiality in all circumstances save when there is a report of child abuse, or a client is determined to be an inherent risk to themselves or someone else. If a client’s risk to themselves or others is serious, foreseeable, and imminent, the ethical responsibility of confidentiality is waived and therapists are responsible for taking appropriate steps to protect the safety of all persons involved.

### Harm to Self

As a clinician, you have a duty to your client to provide a thorough and ongoing assessment of your client's symptomology. Clinicians should screen for suicidal ideation frequently and anytime that depression is indicated by a client. If a client reports suicidal content at any point, whether it be ideation or intention, the clinician should conduct further immediate assessment to determine the risk level of the client.

Clinicians should assess the clients, frequency and severity of suicidal thoughts as well as the imminent risk of the client by determining if the client has a plan, means of completion, and intent to carry out that plan. The Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) is a tool that clinicians can and should utilize to understand the risk of clients facing suicidality.

Regardless of scores shown on the Columbia Suicide Scale or other reported factors, all decisions related to safety and exceptions to confidentiality should be based upon clinical judgment and knowledge of the client, remembering that the client's safety should always remain a top priority.

**Mild Risk Level**

- Passive suicidality
- Thoughts of death without any plans to act on these thoughts.
- No History of suicide attempts.
- Low risk factors for suicide.

If the client reports frequent suicidal ideation regardless of the level of risk, complete a suicide safety plan with the client. Safety plan can be found in Simple Practice and it is recommended you have the client download the ‘Suicide Safety Plan’ app onto their phone to have the plan readily available. Following completing the plan with the client on their phone, add it to Simple Practice to document completion.

Ensure ongoing reassessments are carried out in future sessions. Adapt the client’s treatment plan to address related concerns.

**Moderate Risk Level**

- Specific thoughts of suicide, including potential methods, but without a definite plan or intent.

- May have a history of suicide attempts or self-harm behaviors.

- Presence of multiple risk factors for suicide.

Discuss any lethal means available to the client as part of the safety plan. Arrange and confirm removal or reduction of lethal means as feasible. This may include asking for permission to contact a loved one of the clients to arrange with them the removal or reduction of lethal means. Inform your supervisor of the risk and steps taken to reduce the risk.

Assess that the effectiveness of the current treatment plan and level of care are sufficient to keep the client safe. Make adjustments and recommendations accordingly.

Check in briefly with the client the next business day and assess the current risk level. Ensure ongoing reassessments are carried out in future sessions.

**Severe Risk Level**

- Specific plans for suicide with the intent and means to act on these plans.

- History of previous suicide attempts or serious self-harm behaviors.

- High or escalating risk factors for suicide, including expressions of hopelessness or perceived burdensomeness.

Inform the client of the limits of confidentiality, and encourage them to call a loved one to accompany them to the emergency room or another crisis receiving center. Stay with the client, and do not leave them alone. Remain calm and empathetically engage with the client to encourage them to voluntarily proceed to the emergency room. If a client refuses to take steps for further care, contact emergency contact and/or law enforcement for assistance.

### Harm to Others

In Utah, therapists are held under the duty to warn when a client communicates to the therapist an actual threat of physical violence against a clearly identified or reasonably identifiable victim. If the therapist is made aware of such threats to another person, the therapist should make all reasonable efforts to communicate the threat to the victim and notify a law enforcement officer or agency of the threat. This includes disclosures of intent to harm from both the client and/or client’s family members should follow the same procedure of notifying the possible victim and law enforcement.

There must be a “serious and imminent threat to harm” to trigger a duty to warn. Unless there is a serious and imminent threat, HIPAA privacy standards still prevail. We have a duty to conduct a risk assessment and thoroughly document what we considered in making that assessment.

Any case that presents with reckless or dangerous behavior that may involve danger to self or others should be brought for consultation. Even if no specific threat is made to another person, consult as soon as possible with your supervisor.

**Mild Risk Level**

- Thoughts of violence without any plans to act on these thoughts.
- No history of violent acts or outbursts.
- Low risk factors for homicidality or violence.

If the client reports frequent homicidal ideation regardless of the level of risk, complete a safety plan with the client. Ensure ongoing reassessments are carried out in future sessions. Adapt the client’s treatment plan to address related concerns.

**Moderate Risk Level**

- Specific thoughts of violence including homicidality, including potential methods, but without a definite plan or intent.

- May have a history of violence or impulsivity.

- Presence of multiple risk factors for violence.

Discuss any lethal means available to the client as part of the safety plan. Arrange and confirm removal or reduction of lethal means as feasible. This may include asking for permission to contact a loved one of the clients to arrange with them the removal or reduction of means. Inform your supervisor of the risk and steps taken to reduce the risk.

Assess that the effectiveness of the current treatment plan and level of care are sufficient to keep the client and others safe. Make adjustments and recommendations accordingly.

Check in briefly with the client the next business day and assess the current risk level. Ensure ongoing reassessments are carried out in future sessions.

**Severe**  **Risk Level**

- Specific plans for violence with the intent and means to act on these plans.

- History of previous violence or impulsive behaviors.

- High or escalating risk factors for violence

Begin by ensuring personal safety, excuse yourself from the client and the room, call 911 immediately and seek help from others in the office or nearby businesses. Wait for authorities to respond and follow their direction. If unable to leave the room, focus on seeking help while actively attempting to calm the client.

## Child Abuse Reporting

Whenever any Tangible employee has reason to suspect that a child may have been subjected to abuse or neglect, a report will be made immediately by the employee to your direct supervisor and the Division of Child and Family Services. However, if a child is in immediate danger or if you witness the abuse, call 911.Other wise, Utah’s child abuse reporting hotline is 1(855) 323-3237. Remember that evidence of abuse is not necessary, any reasonable suspicion of abuse should be reported.

A report to a supervisor or colleague does not satisfy the employee’s personal duty to report to law enforcement or DCFS. If a child reports something to you, then **YOU must make the report to the Division of Child and Family Services (DCFS)** . Your supervisor can guide you through the process, but you make the report yourself. You cannot hand the report off to a supervisor or let them decide whether a report should be made. When making the verbal report, always have the person you notify identify himself/herself. The notified person’s name should be noted for documentation purposes.

**Information Needed for Report**

DCFS requires these three pieces of information in order to open and investigate a case:

- The child’s first and last name,
- A location where the child can be found (such as a school, home, or daycare)
- Details of the abuse

Other information that may be helpful to DCFS includes:

- Alleged perpetrator full name and address (if disclosed)
- Names of Parents
- Birthdate of child

### Duty of Investigation

- It is not the responsibility of therapists or other mental health professionals to investigate the legitimacy of the threats or instances of abuse, investigations are the responsibility of law enforcement.
- To determine whether or not there is reason to believe a threat is credible or that abuse has occurred, therapists may (but are not required to) gather information only to the extent necessary to support a reasonable belief that a reportable problem exists.
- Therapists will not contact the client’s parents, relatives, friends, neighbors, or others for the purpose of discussing a report to law enforcement and potential victim or to attempt to determine circumstances surrounding the threat of harm or abuse.
- (Threats of Violence only) Therapists are directed not to contact the client or otherwise give them notice of an investigation regarding threats. All clients are notified of mandatory reporting and limits to confidentiality in the informed consent procedure. It is the responsibility of law enforcement to do all tasks relative to the investigation.
- (Child Abuse) Therapists are directed not to contact parents or otherwise give them notice of an investigation. All clients and parents are notified of mandatory reporting and limits to confidentiality in the informed consent procedure. It is the responsibility of law enforcement or DCFS to do all tasks relative to the investigation. Parents who make inquiries to therapists about a report or an investigation should be directed to DCFS.
- Clients who make inquiries to therapists about a report or an investigation should be directed to law enforcement.

## Crisis Documentation

Following any crisis situation ensure a supervisor is informed and documentation is completed within 24 hours. Document all assessments, risk classifications, decisions made, and actions taken in the client's record. Include details of any safety plans, interventions, and communications with other professionals or emergency services.

## Failure to Report

Failing to follow proper crisis procedures places our clients at risk and creates liability for the clinician and for Tangible. Clinicians found to have violated crisis policies will be immediately investigated and may face termination.

Clinicians can be held legally responsible for failing to report instances of imminent harm and/or child abuse.
**IN THIS LESSON**
# What to cover in a first session
# Before You Start

Starting work with a new client is exciting and we can find ourselves wanting to dive right in. Before we do though, there are a few things that need to be talked about. Setting expectations clearly in the beginning builds trust and avoids confusion and frustration later on.

- Confidentiality- Clients should know the limits of confidentiality and why you may have to break confidentiality.
- Session Length- Sessions are 53-minutes in order to help facilitate confidentiality. Giving time for clients to leave before new clients arrive.
- Billing- Check with the client to see if they know how much their sessions will cost. If they don’t recommend them to call our billing team. All questions regarding billing, payments or cost should be directed to our billing team who can be reached by calling our main number.
- Late Cancel Fee- If the client cancels within 24-hours of the session or doesn’t show up for a session we will charge $75 cancellation fee. The only exception being illness, we don’t want clients coming in sick. That fee cannot be covered by insurance and will be billed directly to the client.
# Explore Away

Once the foundation is set, gently invite the client to share what brings them in. Let them lead, but use open-ended prompts as needed:

- “What made you decide to reach out now?”
- “What’s been feeling heavy or hard lately?”
- “If therapy were helpful, what would that look like for you?”

This part isn’t about gathering every detail, it’s about listening, and beginning to understand their needs, values, and hopes.
# Dig Deeper

Some of the most meaningful work in therapy happens when we gently guide clients beneath the surface, beyond stories they've rehearsed or symptoms they can easily name. Digging deeper means slowing down, listening between the lines, and staying curious about the emotions, beliefs, and experiences that quietly shape their inner world.

This doesn’t mean pushing or prying. It means noticing what’s unsaid, asking thoughtful questions, and creating enough safety for vulnerability to unfold.

*What was the emotion underneath that reaction?*

*Has this dynamic shown up in other relationships too?*

*What would that part of you say if it could speak freely right now?*
# Instilling Hope

Hope is one of the most powerful therapeutic tools we have. As therapists, we hold hope when clients can’t hold it for themselves. We reflect their resilience, remind them of their capacity, and help them envision a life beyond their current pain.

Instilling hope doesn’t mean offering false reassurance or rushing to fix things. It means demonstrating that there is a path forward and you can help them walk it. Talking to clients about a plan and setting out interventions can show that you’re capable of leading them where they want to go.
# Give Homework

When we give homework at the end of a first session it sets a tone, we’re here to change and the change can’t take place solely in the office. The homework shouldn’t be big or overwhelming but should be an invitation to take simple steps that continue the momentum of the session.

Homework can be asking a client to journal, reflect on patterns, reconnect with supports or begin using specific skills. The goal isn’t for the client to solve their problems, it’s to start the client with the right framework, that working on themselves outside of session is a critical step in making change.
**IN THIS LESSON**
# How to engage appropriately with clients.

Tangible’s mantra is “Helping people *feel*  better”. The purpose behind this is to emphasize that our goal as a practice is to teach practical skills that help our clients reconnect/ re-identify with their emotions. Sessions should often employ tangible skills and techniques that keep therapy from becoming an intellectual exercise. We want our clients to leave our office empowered with clear and practical toolsets they can employ.

### Boundaries

Remember, you are a representative of yourself, the practice, and the profession. Your approach should always be professional and should never cross professional boundaries. Self-disclosure should be utilized as a tool and means of building rapport, avoid oversharing or making the session about you.

Your body is your own, you can choose whether a handshake is appropriate or not. Physical contact beyond/other than a handshake is not allowed between therapist and client.
**IN THIS LESSON**

Simple Practice is our client management software. It serves as the hub for all of the work that we do. It is our calendar, our billing software, our place for notes, etc. Knowing how to use it and keep your information accurate will be apart of your daily responsibilities. # How to communicate with the team.
# Talking to Eachother

At Tangible, we use slack as our tool for communicating within our team. It allows us to be able to easily reach out to one another, ask questions, and keep everyone in the loop. You should feel encouraged to use it to stay connected to coworkers as much as to ask professional questions.
# Rules of Slack

- This is a professional space, so while jokes and connection are encouraged here, remember to always keep content appropriate for the workplace.
- Turn on notifications (during work hours) and respond promptly to questions or requests
- Be respectful
- Be a courteous communicator, respond directly to comments instead of in the channel and ask questions in the right channels to avoid excessive notifications.
- Slack is not HIPAA compliant so please do not use client’s identifying information. If needing to refer to a specific client use the first two letters of their first and last name to abbreviate. ie. Client Gr Sc

**IN THIS LESSON**
# Getting clients to book with you.
# What are Consult Calls

Consultation calls are a free service that we offer to help clients make a decision about whether a therapist is a good fit for their needs. The calls are meant to be 15 minutes or less and are there to address the concerns of the clients and help the clients feel comfortable that they are making the right decision to come meet with you.

You should also be assessing, is this client a good fit for you. Do they struggle with things that you can help with? Does this client feel like an appropriate fit for an outpatient setting? Is the client’s personality going to clash with your style? Consults are a great time to make sure you’re working with clients that you want to be working with.

When you have a consult call scheduled, you’ll see it in your calendar along with the name and phone number of the client. They’ll be waiting for your call at the scheduled time so go ahead and give them a ring.
# Mini Session

Consults aren’t meant to be a sales pitch, nor should they be a Q&A, instead think of consults like a mini session. This way the client gets a real idea of what working with you will feel like and you’re not stuck making an awkward sales pitch. Instead do what you do best, be a therapist. Ask questions, validate and form a basic plan with the client of how working with you will help them reach their goals. At the end of the call the client should have a feel of what working with you will feel like and some ideas of what that work will look like.

“If we worked together, what would you be looking to work on?”

“Tell me a little about what you’re hoping to get out of therapy”

“Wow it’s incredible you’ve carried this weight for so long, my suggestion would be that we use a method called EMDR to help relieve the pain of these traumatic memories you have. Let me explain a little what it can do for you…”
# Ready to book?

When you’ve had a chance to talk through everything with the client, ask them if they would like to book an appointment. When it’s a good fit and things go right, the client will be ready to book the appointment on the phone with you. If so, offer them some of the free slots on your calendar and set an appointment with them. Don’t worry about getting them put into simple practice, just set the time, get their name, number, and email address and send it to our receptionist. They’ll take care of the rest.

Sometimes, it’s not the right fit and the client or you may decide that booking a session together isn’t the right choice. That’s ok, don’t be discouraged. You won’t be the right fit for everyone. Ask the client if they would like our receptionist to reach back out to help them find a better fit. Our receptionists are prepared with a list of good therapists both within and outside our practice to help clients find the best match.
**IN THIS LESSON**
# How to work with the reception team
# Responsive Communication

Our reception team is often the first point of contact for your clients, and that first impression matters. Clear, consistent & responsive communication between therapists and reception staff ensures a smooth, welcoming, and professional experience for every client who reaches out for support.

Strong communication helps prevent scheduling mishaps, billing confusion, and logistical delays. It also empowers the reception team to represent you accurately, knowing your preferences, availability, and clinical boundaries so they can support your work effectively. When therapists treat receptionists as integral team members rather than background support the whole system runs smoother.
# What does reception want to know?

In order for our reception team to provide the best service to our clients and to you, they need information from you. Keep your calendar accurate and communicate changes to the reception team. The more information our team has the easier it is for them to be responsive to clients.

- Changes to your schedule, (cancellations, time off, reschedules, etc.)
- If you confirm an online booking request
- Availability and new openings
- Client preferences (Which clients, modalities or personalities do you want to work with)
**IN THIS LESSON**
# The heart of what makes great therapists.
# Be the professional

Our Tangible Tenets are what we believe make great therapists. Please take time to learn about how you can embody these concepts. As you complete this section of our onboarding, you’ll notice your fellow team members and the excited clients who have left reviews for them. We want to highlight the power of great therapists and the great team you’re joining! We know that given time, you will facilitate meaningful change in the lives of your clients here at Tangible.

The way you carry yourself in sessions is as much a therapeutic tool as the words you use. When we act the part it invites trust and engagement from our clients. Conveying a sense of collected confidence is key to helping set the tone for the session. We are the rock in our clients storm, and they will look to us as a steadying force.

# Hone your

# craft

Therapy is a dynamic, evolving field, and staying stagnant doesn’t mean staying still but instead falling behind. Therapy is both an art and a science; honing your craft requires curiosity, humility, and ongoing practice. It reflects a commitment not just to competence, but to excellence. When we invest in our growth, our clients benefit from richer and more transformative work.
# Skill-Based Practice

This is a principle on which Tangible was founded, to give our clients tangible skillsets. Empowerment is the key to our clients success and empowerment starts when we put tools in the hands of our clients. They are the shapers of their future, our job is helping them to see clearly and carry the right tools.
# Plan for success

When we fail to plan, we plan to fail. Success as a therapist doesn’t happen by chance—it’s built through intention, reflection, and a clear vision. Without a clear direction, it's easy to become overwhelmed, burned out, or disconnected from your purpose. Thoughtful planning anchors your work in intention, allowing you to serve your clients more effectively while also honoring your own well-being and goals.
# Follow your heart

While clinical knowledge and technique are essential, intuition brings depth and humanity to the therapeutic process. Learning to follow your heart allows you to attune more fully to your clients’ unspoken needs, shifts in energy, and emotional undercurrents. As you grow in confidence and experience, trusting your intuitive sense can lead to deeper resonance, timely interventions, and a more authentic presence with your clients.
# Self Care

Self-care isn’t a side note; it’s foundational to effective therapy. When therapists are cared for and grounded, they create safer, more attuned spaces for their clients to heal. Neglecting our own needs can lead to burnout and diminished effectiveness. Prioritizing self-care is not only an act of self-respect, but a commitment to showing up fully for the people we serve.
# Customer service

Excellent customer service is an often-overlooked but vital part of therapeutic work. From the first contact to the final session, the way clients are treated shapes their sense of safety, trust, and respect. Clear communication, timely responses, and meaningful gestures ease anxiety and reinforce the importance of the work. Thoughtful service isn’t separate from the healing, it’s part of it.
# Accepting of All

Acceptance in therapy means meeting clients with unconditional respect and understanding; recognizing their inherent worth, emotions, and experiences without judgment. It’s the foundation of a safe therapeutic relationship, where people feel seen and valued exactly as they are. Importantly, acceptance doesn’t mean agreement; therapists can honor the person while not endorsing their actions.
**IN THIS LESSON**
# How to carry yourself as a professional
# Professional Mindset

As therapists, we are entrusted with the mental and emotional well-being of our clients, placing us in a position comparable to that of doctors who care for their patients' physical health. Just like doctors, we possess specialized knowledge and training that enables us to offer a highly skilled and specialized service. It is essential that we approach our work with the same level of responsibility, diligence, and respect for our profession as any healthcare professional.

Firstly, professionalism starts before we ever meet the client in how we manage the administrative aspects of our practice. We must maintain a well-organized schedule, a clean space, and ensure that we are punctual for appointments. Our communication with clients should be timely and refined.
# Professional Attire

Professionalism extends beyond the therapeutic interventions we offer and includes how we present ourselves in our daily practice. From our demeanor to what we wear, how we show up to sessions matters. If you showed up to a doctors office and they were wearing shorts and flip flops, how would that change your perception of them? What about if they were sluggish or stared at their feet the whole appointment? Whether we agree with it or not, how we carry ourselves in sessions impacts our client’s perception of our credibility.

Our attire should convey respect for our clients and the serious nature of the work we do, casual but polished clothing is often the best choice, helping clients feel comfortable while still affirming the professionalism of the therapeutic relationship.
# Professional Demeanor

In sessions, our demeanor should convey that we are a safe and sure place for our clients. Clients come to us in moments of emotional turmoil and uncertainty. They look to us as a steadying presence. We must lean into our professional guidance and expertise to provide our clients with calm and direction. We should arrive at sessions with the gravitas of someone who knows how to help. At times this may mean maintaining an appearance of certainty even in moments we don’t feel certain. Imposter syndrome is a normal part of the job and one that we all experience.

Imagine going to the doctor with a broken arm. You wouldn’t want the doctor to come in and ask you how you think they should heal it. They should come in, give educated explanations about different forms of treatment, and then make a professional recommendation as to what they believe will be most helpful. Similarly, we shouldn’t shy away from making clinical recommendations about treatment “I suggest that we utilize EMDR to address these trauma symptoms.” “I recommend we meet as a family to address this.” “Research shows that ADHD is often best treated through medications and therapy, I suggest you meet with a psychiatrist.”
**IN THIS LESSON**
# When we stop growing, we stop doing good therapy.
# The Craft

In a pottery class, I sat and watched as the instructor shaped a beautiful bowl. She told me that the clay teaches you if you're willing to listen. I watched as she shaped the bowl on the wheel, her hands steady but soft, adjusting pressure with each subtle shift in the clay’s movement. The piece looked finished more than once, but she kept turning, refining, smoothing—responding not to a formula, but to what the clay asked of her in real time.

Therapy is no different. It is a living craft, shaped by each client’s unique rhythm and story. Clients don’t come with roadmaps, and therapy isn’t one-size-fits-all. Each session invites nuance, flexibility, and sometimes even the courage to sit with not knowing. To grow in this work is to stay in relationship with it—to keep listening, adjusting, learning. While your graduate training may have laid the foundation, true mastery develops over time. Honing your craft isn’t about chasing perfection; it’s about deepening your capacity to show up with skill, integrity, and attunement.
# How to Hone

Honing your craft begins with a commitment to lifelong learning. Attend trainings, read current literature, and explore modalities that challenge and excite you. Whether it’s deepening in a specific approach like EMDR or learning something new like IFS, staying curious keeps your work fresh and relevant.

Outside perspectives help illuminate blind spots and offer valuable feedback. Specifically, inviting feedback from clients can help you find areas to improve. Engage effectively with supervision and make sure it’s a space that works for you. Supervision isn’t just about staffing cases. It’s your own personalized training ground, so take advantage and ask for trainings that fit your goals.

Make time to think critically about your sessions—what worked, what didn’t, and what felt unclear. Reflection builds insight, intuition, and confidence over time.
**IN THIS LESSON**
# Tangible skills, it’s who we are.
# Empowerment

A skill-based therapy practice centers on equipping clients with practical tools they can carry into their daily lives—not just insight, but action. It means therapy doesn’t stay in the office; it moves with the client into their lives. While processing the past and understanding patterns remains essential, skill-based therapy emphasizes empowering clients with the tools they need to create meaningful change.
# Concrete Skills

Our approach focuses on the development of concrete, repeatable techniques clients can use between sessions. Whether it’s learning how to set boundaries, challenge unhelpful thoughts, or regulate intense emotions, a skill-based practice helps clients build self-efficacy and resilience. It reflects a belief that healing involves not just being heard, but creating change.

To be effective, use methods that are teachable, measurable, and adaptable. Sessions should include the use and practice of skills, not just the teaching of them. Rather than sending a link of a meditation to a client after the session, take time in the session to guide them through a meditation together. Don’t be afraid to spend large portions of a session practicing skills together.
# Giving Homework

Each session should end with work the client can do between sessions to continue their progress. Homework in therapy plays a vital role in bridging the gap between insight and change. While powerful moments can happen in session, lasting growth often comes from what clients practice and reflect on between sessions. Thoughtfully assigned homework—whether it’s journaling, trying a new coping skill, or observing patterns—helps reinforce learning, deepen self-awareness, and build momentum. It empowers clients to take an active role in their healing and fosters a sense of ownership in the therapeutic process.
**IN THIS LESSON**
# Great therapy starts with a plan.
# Direction and Purpose

Therapy is most effective when it has a clear sense of direction. Without it, sessions can become repetitive, and meaningful progress may stall. A thoughtful plan gives the work shape, helping both client and therapist stay aligned and intentional.

Planning also invites collaboration. Clients feel more engaged when they know where they’re headed and how far they’ve come. For therapists, it offers clarity and focus, serving as a steady guide through the therapeutic process.
# Start with Values

Effective planning begins with understanding what matters most to your client. Beyond symptom relief, what kind of life are they trying to build? What does “better” look like for them? Starting with values creates motivation and anchors the work in something personally meaningful.
# Set measurable goals

Work with clients to create goals that are specific, realistic, and measurable. Instead of “I want to feel less anxious,” help reframe that as “I want to go to social events twice a month without leaving early.” Clear goals help you select appropriate interventions and give clients a way to track their own growth.
# Start where your clients is

Effective therapy isn’t about applying the same technique to every situation—it’s about choosing interventions that resonate with each client’s unique personality, goals, and context. What works for one client may feel flat or overwhelming to another.

Matching your approach means tuning into your client’s values, communication style, and readiness for change. It’s a blend of clinical skill and relational attunement, where interventions aren’t just evidence-based, but person-centered. When clients feel truly seen and the tools align with their needs, therapy becomes more engaging, meaningful, and impactful.
# Follow the plan

It can be tempting to introduce new techniques or switch directions frequently, especially when you're excited about a recent training or feeling pressure to “make progress.” But constantly shifting approaches without anchoring to a clear plan can confuse clients and dilute the effectiveness of the work. Therapy isn’t about chasing novelty, it’s about consistency, depth, and trust in the process.

Sticking to the plan doesn’t mean being rigid. It means committing to the goals you’ve set together and staying the course long enough to see real change. When adjustments are needed, they should be intentional and collaborative, not reactive. Clients benefit most when therapy is focused, grounded, and paced with purpose, not driven by passing impulse.
**IN THIS LESSON**
# Creating a space where all people feel  cared for.
# The power behind therapy

At the core of every effective therapeutic relationship is acceptance; a deep, unwavering respect for each client’s humanity, no matter their story, background, or identity. Being a therapist means holding space for people in all their complexity: their pain, their growth, their contradictions, and their dreams. True acceptance doesn’t mean agreeing with everything a client says or does; rather, it’s about creating an environment where they feel seen, safe, and valued exactly as they are in that moment.

When clients sense genuine acceptance, they begin to relax into authenticity. They’re more likely to explore difficult emotions, question long-held beliefs, and confront experiences they’ve kept hidden. Acceptance communicates, “You don’t have to earn my respect or compassion.” This message can be especially healing for individuals who have experienced rejection due to their race, gender, sexuality, faith, body, or neurodiversity. In therapy, acceptance becomes a corrective emotional experience—a place where clients are no longer defined by their wounds, but by their capacity to heal.
# Celebrate difference

Acceptance goes far beyond tolerance. Tolerance implies allowing difference; acceptance celebrates it. As therapists, our role is to actively honor the diverse lived experiences that each client brings into the room. This means doing our own inner work; examining biases, expanding cultural awareness, and being open to learning from perspectives that differ from our own. A spirit of humility allows us to see every client as the expert of their own experience, while we hold space as guides and companions on their path toward growth.
# Know your biases

Practicing acceptance begins with self-awareness. Therapists who are attuned to their own emotions and biases are better equipped to stay grounded and open with clients. This means noticing our internal reactions, when we feel judgment, discomfort, or frustration, and gently exploring them without shame. Judgement and discernment can be powerful therapeutic tools when used correctly. Supervision, consultation, and personal therapy are invaluable spaces to process these responses so they don’t unconsciously shape our interactions.
# Support clients, not behaviors

**Disclaimer: This section does not apply to client identities. Being LGBT or a part of another minority group is not harmful behavior. Harm befalling a person due to their identity is not the fault of the identity holder.**

A common misconception about acceptance is that it means approval; that to accept someone, we must agree with everything they do. A critical component of therapy is therapeutic accountability, or the skill to pushback on ideas that are unhelpful or harmful to the client. Acceptance is not the same as endorsement and we should be mindful not to encourage harmful behaviors or patterns.

Acceptance still involves maintaining therapeutic accountability while staying compassionate. We can validate a client’s emotional reality (“It sounds like you were trying to protect yourself”) without validating the behavior itself (“That choice caused real harm, and it’s important we look at that together”). When therapists model this balance—empathy with accountability—we teach clients to hold the same nuanced compassion for themselves. They learn that they can face their own mistakes without collapsing into guilt or defensiveness, which opens the door to genuine growth.
**IN THIS LESSON**
# Letting intuition be your guide.
# The art of therapy

Therapy is often described as both an art and a science—and it’s in the “art” that we find the beating heart of the work. While evidence-based practices and theory are essential, some of the most powerful moments in therapy don’t come from textbooks. They come from the therapist’s presence, courage, and capacity to follow their heart.

But what does that actually mean? And how can we distinguish between impulsive reactions and wise, intuitive guidance?
# Listening to Intuition

Intuition in therapy is that subtle, often wordless sense of “something” arising in the room. A nudge to ask a deeper question, a quiet pause before offering a reflection, a gut sense that there’s more to the story than what’s being said. Intuition can’t be forced—but it can be cultivated.

Following your heart as a therapist means learning to listen to this inner compass without needing to immediately justify it with logic. It means trusting that your felt sense, shaped by experience and deep attunement, has value. Of course, intuition must be held alongside ethics, supervision, and clinical judgment—but when used skillfully, it can lead to profound insight and connection.
# Counter transference

Often, the heart speaks through countertransference. The emotional responses you experience in the presence of a client: frustration, protectiveness, longing, tension. They aren’t distractions; they’re data. While countertransference can reflect your own wounds, it can also be a guide to what's happening in the relational field.

Following your heart doesn’t mean acting on every feeling—it means being curious about them. What are your emotions trying to tell you about the client’s experience? About your own boundaries or history? When explored thoughtfully, countertransference can illuminate blind spots, deepen empathy, and enrich the therapeutic alliance.
# Being Courageous

Following your heart may feel risky, especially in a field that often prioritizes technique over intuition. But your presence, your genuine, attuned, heartfelt presence, is one of the most healing tools you have. Following your heart as a therapist isn’t about abandoning structure or reason; it’s about weaving them with wisdom, humanity, and deep listening. Intuition and countertransference are not distractions from the work, they *are*  the work, when we have the courage to pay attention.

Trust your training. Trust the process. And trust that your heart, when grounded and open, knows the way.
**IN THIS LESSON**
# Taking care of our most vital resource, you.
# Progress not Perfection

At Tangible, we care that our therapists try their best in each session, not that each session goes perfectly. You’re only human which means you’ll have off days, bad sessions and make mistakes. Our goal is to see you as a sum of your parts rather than one bad day and we hope you offer yourself the same grace.

We ask our therapists to grow, to lead with their hearts and to lean into courageous actions. That means that sometimes you’re going to miss the mark. You may lose clients cause of mistakes you make. That’s ok. Unless it becomes a pattern we won’t worry about it and neither should you. Be compassionate with yourself on hard days and remember we believe in you.
# Don’t outwork your clients

It’s easy to fall into the trap of over-investing, especially when you care deeply. But if you find yourself working harder than your clients, staying up thinking about their problems, or feeling responsible for their outcomes, it’s time to pause.

You cannot want change more than your clients do. Your job is to walk alongside them, not carry them. Overfunctioning not only drains you, but it can rob clients of their agency and growth. Respecting their responsibility in the process is an act of trust and empowerment. If you find disengagement, barriers or resistance to the work. address it. Don’t take their lack of progression on yourself.
# Know your limits

You are not infinite. There is a threshold beyond which your care becomes unsustainable, your focus blurs, and your presence suffers. Knowing how much you can truly handle, emotionally, logistically, energetically, is crucial.

This might mean setting a firm client cap, spacing out certain types of sessions, or building in breaks to your schedule. It might also mean saying no, even when you feel guilty. Overextending yourself doesn’t make you a better therapist, it puts you at risk for burnout.
# Work-life balance

This is not your life, this is your job, and we understand that. For some, therapy may feel like a calling and we love that for you. We want your priorities to always be your life before your work. Rest, play, connection, and joy are not indulgences, they’re necessary. Creating work-life balance means designing a practice that honors both your personal needs and professional goals.

Limit work communication outside of your hours, take regular vacations, and build rituals that help you transition out of “therapist mode.” The more nourished you are outside the office, the more grounded and effective you’ll be inside it.
**IN THIS LESSON**
# The little things that make the difference
# First Impressions

Before a client even sits on your couch (or logs into your video session), they’re already forming impressions; based on our website, the intake process, your responsiveness. Do they feel welcomed? Informed? Respected?

When communication is timely, forms are clear, and onboarding feels smooth, clients experience a sense of safety before the clinical work even begins. Good customer service helps lower anxiety and build trust right from the start.
# Consistency Builds Trust

Being on time, following through on what you say, and returning messages within a reasonable timeframe, all of these seemingly small actions communicate professionalism and reliability.

They reinforce the idea that you’re not just a caring person, but someone who can be counted on. And for clients who may have experienced inconsistency, chaos, or relational breaches in the past, this consistency can be quietly reparative.
# Clear Communication

Clients deserve to understand what they’re stepping into, fees, policies, boundaries, expectations. Clear communication fosters empowerment and reduces the chance of misunderstanding. Take time during your first session to ensure the client is meeting with informed consent.

Transparent customer service isn’t about perfection; it’s about being thoughtful and responsive. When things are clear, clients can focus on the work instead of worrying about logistics.
# Mistakes Happen

No matter how intentional or organized you are, mistakes will happen. Maybe you forget to send a link, double-book a session, misspeak in session, or fail to follow up as promised. In therapy, how you respond to those moments matters just as much, if not more, than the mistake itself.

Repair is a powerful relational act. When you take ownership, offer a sincere apology, and clarify how you’ll prevent the issue moving forward, you reinforce trust rather than damage it. When mistakes happen, attempt to resolve them and let your supervisor know so they can help if needed.
